messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Two years ago, during a routine convoy stop, a buried charge detonated beside Caleb’s vehicle. The concussive force threw him against the harness, immediately followed by the rhythmic thumping of a gunship returning to suppress enemy positions overhead. The air grew thick with the acrid, chemical tang of scorched metal and burning tires. He pulled himself out through shattered glass, but the sequence of violence never fully assembled in his mind. It remained a collection of disconnected fragments that did not fit together, and though he knew what happened, he simply could not find words to describe it. In the months since his medical discharge, those unplaceable memories stopped behaving like fragments. They began playing over and over in his head, a relentless film he could not pause. His unshakable belief that his life is not worth living anymore filtered his recall, making the memories feel inescapable rather than distant. Because he was certain that the world is a dangerous place, Caleb found himself retreating into his phone, spending long hours on games and the internet to avoid thinking. The memories, playing their endless loop, actively drove him toward these digital screens; when the replay grew too loud, he would lock the route on his map and drown out his own mind. His job as a city bus driver became a gauntlet of sensory triggers. On a Tuesday morning, a car backfired near the intersection, and the sudden auditory cue of an explosion or bang sounds made him jerk the wheel, his breath catching as the noise mirrored the desert. He pulled over, waiting for the phantom rhythm of a helicopter or aircraft sounds to join the noise, his hands gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles turned white. The smell of the bus’s diesel exhaust sometimes thickened in the cabin, a burnt smell that instantly transported him back to the scorched vehicle. Because of these invasions, he began avoiding crowded places such as shopping centres or public events, and he stopped attending his family’s church, steering clear of places of worship or religious gatherings that reminded him of the silence after gunfire. The unrelenting replay of the event did more than startle him; it cemented his negative appraisals. Every time the fragmented pieces resurfaced, they reinforced his conviction that the world is a dangerous place, leaving him feeling he had to be on guard all the time. Conversely, his own coping mechanisms worked against him. By spending long hours on his phone to escape the pain, he never processed the trauma, and this digital escape ensured that the memories remained sharp and unaddressed. The avoidance of crowds and religious spaces left him increasingly isolated, while his supervisors noted the missed stops and distracted driving. His sister’s texts went unanswered, and the hypervigilance that kept him on guard all the time siphoned off his energy. By the time Caleb walked into the clinic, he had run out of routes to hide behind. He was tired of the constant guard, tired of the phone screen glowing in the dark, and tired of the way his life had shrunk. He came in hoping for a way to make the film stop, or at least to understand why the burnt smell in a gas station parking lot could still make his heart stop. He was most afraid that talking would only pull the fragments back together, but he hoped someone might finally help him find the words he had lost, so he could at least try to believe that his life is worth living again.
